column4: The source section’s root ص ل ي means entering and enduring fire; 4:56 uses nuslihim, then says skins cook and are replaced so the punishment continues.
The section gives the dictionary form شويته (I roasted it); 18:29 uses يشوي for water like molten metal scorching faces, after the Prophet is told to state the choice to believe or disbelieve.
This single verse sets rivers of pleasant drinks in the Garden beside the disbelievers’ boiling water that tears their entrails, sharpening the contrast with 88:5’s spring.
The section explains ء ن ي as heat that has reached its utmost; 55:44 names ḥamīmin ān and places it between Hellfire and its people.
The section quotes this exact name, nārun ḥāmiyah, for the hot fire; it makes the measured judgment in Sūrat al-Qāriʿah end in this heat.
The source explicitly compares this previous surah’s yataslā naran kubrā with 88:4: the same ص ل ي root marks the one who enters the great fire.
The source quotes lā yaṣlāhā illā al-ashqā; it uses the same ص ل ي root as 88:4 and identifies who enters the fire.
The section links 88:4’s fire with 88:23’s turning away and disbelief; this next ayah identifies the condemned as one who denied and turned away, repeating tawallā.
The section names 88:5’s root ء ن ي for a meal reaching readiness; 33:53 says guests should not wait for its inā, and joins that cooking-time word to food and looking.
The source’s ص ل ي root is both enduring fire and roasting; 4:10 pictures those who wrongfully consume orphans’ property as eating fire in their bellies and then burning in the blaze.
The verse uses nuslihi for burning in Hell after someone turns against the Messenger and follows another way; its tawallā root also meets 88:23’s turning away.
The section explains ḥāmiyah with iron heated in fire; 9:35 uses the same ḥ-m-y root for heated gold and silver, then for cauterizing faces, sides, and backs.
This ayah clothes the disbelieving group in Fire; 22:20 adds boiling water poured over their heads that melts bellies and skins, continuing the bodily heat in the section.
Here boiling water is poured over heads and melts what is in bellies and skins, a bodily cooking scene that gives the section’s heat, drink, and food sharper physical form.
The section’s thorn is the only food in 88:6; this passage names Zaqqum as the food of the sinner before describing what it does in the next ayat.
The molten-metal comparison boils in the belly, turning the section’s cooking vocabulary into an image of the sinner’s food becoming torment.
44:46 intensifies that boiling by comparing it to the boil of ḥamīm, completing 44:45’s molten food image with hot water.
After the sinner is seized in the Zaqqum passage, boiling water is poured over his head; the hot spring is applied to the body as well as drunk.
The question “is this a better reception” introduces the tree of Zaqqum as the food awaiting sinners, extending 88:6’s theme of a hostile meal.
The sinners eat from Zaqqum and fill their bellies; this adds an act of consuming to the section’s thorn that cannot satisfy hunger.
37:67 adds a scalding drink on top of that food, matching the section’s pairing of a harmful meal with a painfully hot spring.
The condemned are made to eat from Zaqqum, a second Qur’anic image of punishment as a meal rather than nourishment.
56:53 says they fill their bellies from that tree; the detail makes the meal’s apparent quantity cruelly different from the thorn that cannot relieve hunger.
After the Zaqqum meal they drink boiling water, continuing the food-and-hot-drink sequence that the section links to 88:5’s hot spring and 88:6’s thorn meal.
This is the verse quoted in the section: the drinkers take water like thirst-sick camels, making their desperate drinking part of the torment.
After the meal and drink, 56:56 calls this their reception on Judgment Day; it turns the section’s kitchen and meal language into a deliberately cruel hospitality.
This ayah gives the person a reception of boiling water, echoing the section’s hot spring and the passage’s own language of a meal or welcome.
The section’s ص ل ي entry includes roasting meat; here tasliyatu jaḥīm names burning in Hell, joining the secondary cooking sense to its primary punishment sense.
Those who treated religion as play are assigned a drink of ḥamīm and painful punishment, a concrete parallel to the section’s hot spring.
After describing resurrection and recompense, the verse assigns disbelievers a drink of ḥamīm; it ties the section’s hot drink to denial and judgment.
The condemned are plunged into boiling water and then kindled in the fire, giving the section’s spring and fire as successive punishments.
The condemned find neither coolness nor drink; 78:25 makes the drink boiling water, a precise reversal of relief from thirst.
78:25 names only ḥamīm and ghassāq as drink, specifying the deprivation that 78:24 sets up.
When the condemned are thrown into the Fire, it is heard boiling; the cauldron-like fire fits the section’s furnace and cooking language.
The verse says there is no food except ghislīn, a direct parallel to the section’s denial of ordinary food in favor of a harmful substitute.
69:37 restricts that food to sinners, completing the previous ayah’s account of the condemned diet.
Alongside shackles and blazing fire, this verse gives choking food; it adds the bodily difficulty of eating to 88:6’s thorn diet.
The section calls a heated cooking oven a tannūr; in Noah’s flood the same noun marks the place from which water erupts, joining the oven image to the flood’s beginning.
This retelling again makes the tannūr the point where floodwater erupts; it repeats the section’s heated-oven word at the threshold between fire and water.

The drink in this passage is swallowed only with difficulty, and death does not release the drinker; it extends the section’s torment through a drink that cannot bring relief, though this water is not called boiling.
The same ص ل ي root used in 88:4 appears in the promise to place an unjust aggressor in the Fire, extending the section’s act of entering punishment to another stated cause.
The root ص ل ي appears in the statement that God knows best who is most deserving of burning there; the verse makes the fire an assigned judgment, not merely an image of heat.
The phrase ṣālī al-jaḥīm uses the same root as the section’s entry into fire for those destined for Hell.
This verse says that the wrongdoers burn in Hell and calls it a wretched resting place; yaslawnahā is the same root the section explains through entering and enduring fire.
The verse warns that those who persist in hostile secret counsel will burn in a blazing fire; yaslawn is the same burning root named by the section.
The one who receives his record from behind burns in the blaze; yaslā is the same root as 88:4’s taslā.
The section says the hot fire in 101:11 is for one whose scales are light; this ayah supplies that person and the failed measure.
101:9 assigns the light-scaled person Hawiyah, the destination that 101:11 identifies as a blazing hot fire.
God commands the fire to become cool and safe for Abraham: this reverses the section’s defining property of a hot fire while keeping the same element.
In the Garden of Adam, hunger is absent; that is the exact bodily opposite of a meal that cannot relieve hunger in 88:7.
The Garden also excludes thirst and exposure to the sun’s heat, reversing the section’s hot spring and bodily exposure to torment.
The people of the Fire beg the people of the Garden for water and provision but are refused; this clarifies the deprivation behind being given a boiling spring.
The section names 88:3’s root ن ص ب for exhausting labor; here the people of the lasting Garden say no naṣab touches them, reversing that weariness.
The Garden has no naṣab or expulsion; the same root contrasts with the section’s nāṣibah, the laboring and weary face.
Job calls his suffering nuṣb and torment; the same root the section uses for weariness here names affliction, a related but distinct hardship.
The section’s dictionary branch pictures a bird walking into a trap it has set; this verse says evil plotting encircles only its authors, a precise self-caught relation behind the fire image.
The command fansab uses the section’s root ن ص ب for strenuous effort, though its devotional exertion differs from 88:3’s weariness and the dictionary’s pot support.
The Garden’s inhabitants are told to eat and drink in satisfaction, the opposite of a thorn that cannot nourish or relieve hunger.
The Garden’s people are welcomed to eat and drink in comfort, reversing the section’s meal and drink as torment.
Fruit and desired meat are supplied to the Garden’s people, a specific opposite to the sole thorn food in 88:6.
In the same surah that describes drinking like thirsting camels, the Garden has cups passed around from a flowing source, reversing the boiling drink.
The Garden’s drink causes neither harm nor loss of sense, opposite to water that inflicts torment in the section’s image.
The Garden serves fruit of the kind they choose, contrasting with the section’s single thorn food.
The Garden serves flesh of birds they desire, a concrete meal opposite to food that cannot nourish.
The Garden’s cup is carried around from a flowing spring, a specific reversal of the hot spring in the section and the Zaqqum passage later in this surah.
The Garden drink is clear and pleasant to drinkers, opposite to water whose defining feature is unbearable heat.
The cup brings no harm or intoxication, giving bodily relief opposite to the harmful drink in the Hell passage later in the surah.
The righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, a pleasant beverage opposite to the boiling water served to the condemned.
That drink comes from a spring the righteous can make flow, contrasting with an extreme-hot spring assigned as punishment.
The section notes that ص ل ي can describe roasting meat; here Abraham brings guests a roasted calf, showing ordinary food hospitality against the section’s punitive cooking image.
The Fire scorches the wrongdoers’ faces, extending the bodily burning in the section from skin to the visible face.
This ayah calls the punishment a blazing fire; 70:16 says it strips the scalp, making the section’s hot fire a bodily attack.
This ayah describes the blaze stripping the scalp, a concrete bodily effect that continues 70:15’s fire scene.
The speaker says he will burn the man in Saqar; uṣlīhi uses the same ص ل ي root as 88:4.
Saqar is described as scorching the skin, a direct bodily cooking effect alongside the section’s hot fire.
The verse pictures pitch-like garments and faces covered by fire, adding clothing and facial surfaces to the section’s account of bodily burning.
The section’s ص ل ي root covers enduring fire and roasting; 69:31 uses it in the command to burn the condemned in Hell, immediately before the passage describes his lack of food.

The section’s culinary image makes Hell a place of false food; this verse depicts those concealing revelation as eating nothing but fire into their bellies, a distinct image of punishment consumed from within.
After eating Zaqqum and drinking scalding water in 37:66–67, they return to Hell; this closes the food-and-drink sequence by bringing it back to the fire.
This verse places the condemned in scorching wind and boiling water, adding an enveloping hot atmosphere to the section’s hot spring and fire.
After 70:15–16 names the blazing fire and its effect on the scalp, this verse says it calls those who turned away; its tawallā directly echoes 88:23’s turning away.
The one who shuns the reminder is called the most wretched, immediately before 87:12 says he enters the great fire; this clarifies the turn away from reminder behind the section’s fire and 88:23.
The next verse says the one who enters the great fire neither dies nor lives, completing the fate introduced in the section’s cited 87:12 and extending its unrelieved torment.
This verse warns the hearer of a blazing fire; 92:15 then names the one who burns in it, giving the section’s cited burning verse its warning context.
This ayah identifies Hell as what the criminals denied; 55:44 then places them between it and extreme-hot water, linking denial to the section’s fire and spring.
This verse names their shade as black smoke; 56:44 says it is neither cool nor beneficial, completing the hot environment that 56:42 began.
The condemned man had not urged feeding the poor; 69:36 then gives him no food except ghislīn, making the afterlife diet a pointed reversal of his neglect of others’ hunger.
Saqar is said to leave nothing and spare nothing, a specific account of fire’s consuming force that extends the section’s hot-fire image.
The section links hot fire to heated metal; 55:35 sends a flame and nuḥās against humans. If nuḥās means molten copper, it extends that hot-metal image, though it can also mean smoke.
The shade is neither cool nor beneficial, making the absence of relief explicit beside the section’s defining heat and boiling drink.

The one who fears will heed the reminder, opposite the one who shuns it in 87:11 and then enters the fire in 87:12; this gives a positive boundary to the section’s link between turning away and punishment.
Immediately after 92:15–16 describes burning and denial, the most God-fearing is kept away from that fire, making the passage’s opposite fate explicit.
